name: Gastrocnemius
func: The two-headed muscle that forms the bulge of the calf. It points the foot down to push off when walking, running and jumping, and also helps bend the knee.

levels.kid:
Feel the back of your lower leg. That round bump is your **calf**, and the big muscle making it is the **gastrocnemius**.

It has **two parts** side by side, like two hands holding the back of your knee. They join into a thick cord at your heel called the **Achilles tendon**.

When this muscle squeezes, it pulls your heel up so you **stand on tiptoe**. It pushes you forward every time you **walk, run and jump**. Its name comes from Greek words meaning "belly of the leg", because it bulges out.
levels.hs:
The **gastrocnemius** is the most superficial muscle of the **back (posterior compartment)** of the leg and forms the visible bulge of the calf. It lies right under the skin, covering the flatter **soleus** muscle beneath it.

It has two heads. The **medial head** (the larger) starts on the back of the femur just above the **medial condyle**, and the **lateral head** starts just above the **lateral condyle**. The two heads form the lower borders of the **popliteal fossa** behind the knee. They join, and halfway down the leg their tendon merges with soleus's tendon to form the **calcaneal (Achilles) tendon**, which inserts on the back of the **calcaneus** (heel bone).

Together, gastrocnemius and soleus are called the **triceps surae**.

Actions: gastrocnemius is the main **plantarflexor** of the ankle (pointing the foot down), producing powerful push-off in running and jumping. Because it crosses the knee, it also helps **flex the knee**. It works best when the knee is straight.

It is supplied by the **tibial nerve** (S1–S2). Tapping the Achilles tendon gives the **ankle reflex**, which tests **S1**.
levels.college:
**Attachments:** medial head from the posterior femur above the medial condyle; lateral head from the lateral surface of the lateral condyle. A small sesamoid bone, the **fabella**, is present in the lateral head tendon in a minority of people (prevalence varies widely by population). Insertion: via the calcaneal tendon onto the middle part of the posterior surface of the calcaneus.

**Relations:** in the popliteal fossa, the heads lie superficial to the **popliteal artery and vein** and the **tibial nerve**. The **small saphenous vein** runs up the back of the calf in the groove between the two heads, accompanied by the **sural nerve**, before piercing the deep fascia to join the popliteal vein. Deep to gastrocnemius lie soleus and the slender **plantaris**, whose long thin tendon runs between them.

**Innervation:** branches of the **tibial nerve** (S1–S2) given off in the popliteal fossa. **Blood supply:** **sural arteries** from the popliteal artery, one to each head; each head is a separate unit with its own artery, important in muscle flaps.

**Function:** gastrocnemius has mainly **type II** (fast) fibres compared with soleus, so it contributes most to explosive actions such as sprinting and jumping, while soleus maintains posture. Because it crosses the knee, its plantarflexion strength depends on knee angle: with the knee flexed it is slack, so soleus does most of the work.

**Calf muscle pump:** contraction of the calf muscles squeezes the deep veins, and one-way valves direct blood upward toward the heart. This "peripheral heart" is essential for venous return when standing and walking.
levels.phd:
The Achilles tendon formed by gastrocnemius and soleus is the strongest tendon in the body, experiencing forces of several times body weight during running (estimates often range from 6 to 12 times). It is a crucial elastic structure: during running, it stretches in early stance and recoils during push-off, returning a large fraction of the energy, which lowers metabolic cost. Ultrasound studies show the **muscle fascicles** of the medial gastrocnemius may remain nearly the same length (nearly isometric) during this phase while the tendon does the lengthening and shortening, a "**catapult**" mechanism that lets muscle generate force economically.

The Achilles tendon twists as it descends: fibres from the medial gastrocnemius rotate to insert laterally, and soleus fibres more medially. This creates three **subtendons** that can slide relative to each other, enabling somewhat independent action. Research suggests ageing reduces this sliding, possibly contributing to tendon injury.

Gastrocnemius has a **pennate** structure with relatively short fascicles. Its medial head shows greater force-generating capacity. In humans, compared with apes, the Achilles tendon is long and the muscle belly short and high on the leg, an adaptation linked to efficient bipedal running.

The **ankle reflex** involves Ia afferents synapsing on S1 motor neurons. The **H-reflex**, an electrical analogue recorded from soleus and gastrocnemius by stimulating the tibial nerve, is widely used in neurophysiology to test spinal excitability, including changes after spinal cord injury and during learning.
levels.expert:
**Exam:** inspect calf bulk, ask the patient to stand on tiptoe on one leg repeatedly, and test the **ankle reflex (S1)**. Loss of the ankle reflex with weak plantarflexion and numbness of the lateral foot suggests **S1 radiculopathy**.

**Achilles tendon rupture** classically happens in middle-aged weekend athletes during sudden push-off, felt as a "kick" to the back of the heel. Signs: a palpable gap 2–6 cm above the insertion, weak plantarflexion and a positive **Thompson (Simmonds) test**: squeezing the calf does not plantarflex the foot. Some active plantarflexion may still be possible via other muscles, so don't be fooled. Ultrasound or MRI helps when unclear. Both surgical repair and functional bracing are used; modern studies show similar re-rupture rates with accelerated rehabilitation.

**Medial gastrocnemius strain** ("tennis leg") causes sudden pain in the mid-calf, often in middle-aged players.

**Deep vein thrombosis** in the calf veins presents with swelling, warmth and tenderness; it is diagnosed with compression ultrasound and D-dimer testing, guided by clinical scores such as **Wells**. A ruptured **Baker's cyst** from the knee can mimic DVT by tracking between the gastrocnemius heads.

**Compartment syndrome** of the superficial posterior compartment can follow trauma.

**Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome** occurs when an abnormal medial gastrocnemius head compresses the artery, causing calf pain on exercise in young athletes.

**Gastrocnemius tightness** contributes to equinus, toe-walking and plantar fasciitis. In cerebral palsy, **gastrocnemius recession** lengthens the tendon. The **medial gastrocnemius flap** is a workhorse for covering wounds around the knee.

keyPoints: Two heads from the femoral condyles; forms the calf bulge
Joins soleus to form the Achilles tendon (triceps surae)
Plantarflexes the ankle and helps flex the knee
Tibial nerve S1–S2; ankle reflex tests S1

test.q: Which tendon connects the gastrocnemius to the heel?
test.explain: Gastrocnemius and soleus join to form the Achilles tendon.

test.q: Gastrocnemius and soleus together are called the triceps ______.
Squeezing the calf fails to plantarflex the foot. This positive test indicates:
Why does gastrocnemius contribute less to plantarflexion when the knee is bent?
choices: It is slack because it crosses the knee
test.explain: As a two-joint muscle, gastrocnemius is shortened when the knee flexes.

test.q: The ankle reflex mainly tests which spinal root?
test.explain: An absent ankle reflex points to S1 radiculopathy or neuropathy.
